```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(gradethis)
library(learnr)
library(reticulate)

# Exercises graded on a value instead of the exact code.
# Add an entry here to opt an exercise in, using list(var) to check a variable,
# list(expr) to check a Python expression, or list(last_value = TRUE) to check the
# student's last line. The result is compared against the same thing computed from
# the exercise's -solution chunk; add value = ... to compare against a fixed number
# instead. Add defines = "name" to require the student's code to define that name
# itself. Any exercise not listed is graded by exact code match against its
# -solution chunk.
value_checks <- list(
  # The summary table from .describe() (or anything with the same values)
  ex13 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  mean = list(var = "mean_mcds", defines = "mean_mcds"),
  # np.std() without ddof = 1 gives the population standard deviation, which won't match
  sd = list(var = "std_mcds", defines = "std_mcds"),
  n = list(last_value = TRUE),
  se = list(var = "se_mcds", defines = "se_mcds"),
  # The 2.5th percentile (a negative t*) works just as well as the 97.5th, so compare sizes
  ex30 = list(expr = "abs(t_star)", defines = "t_star"),
  ex31 = list(expr = "abs(MoE_mcds)", defines = "MoE_mcds"),
  ex32 = list(expr = paste(
    'int(bool(np.isclose(lower_mcds, mean_mcds - abs(MoE_mcds)))',
    'and bool(np.isclose(upper_mcds, mean_mcds + abs(MoE_mcds))))'),
    value = 1, defines = c("lower_mcds", "upper_mcds")),
  # t.interval() returns a (lower, upper) tuple
  ex34 = list(last_value = TRUE)
)

# Python helpers for custom_checker (done in Python so they work the same on every
# Python version).
# get_result runs code like learnr does (setup objects visible, new variables kept
# separate) and returns the value being checked.
# values_match compares a student's result to the expected one. Data frames and
# series match if they have the same row labels and values, ignoring their names and
# row order. Tuples and lists match if each of their elements match.
checker_py <- '
# (imports go inside the functions because py_run_string keeps top-level names local)
def get_result(code, var=None, expr=None, last_value=False, defines=()):
    import ast
    import __main__
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    if last_value:
        if not tree.body:
            raise ValueError("no code")
        last = tree.body[-1]
        if isinstance(last, ast.Assign) and len(last.targets) == 1 and isinstance(last.targets[0], ast.Name):
            # Last line is `name = expr`, so read `name`
            var = last.targets[0].id
        elif isinstance(last, ast.Expr):
            # Rewrite the last line `expr` as `__check_result__ = expr` so we can read it
            target = ast.Name(id="__check_result__", ctx=ast.Store())
            tree.body[-1] = ast.copy_location(ast.Assign(targets=[target], value=last.value), last)
            ast.fix_missing_locations(tree)
            var = "__check_result__"
        else:
            raise ValueError("last line is not an expression")
    user_vars = {}
    # Plotting code ends in plt.show(), which could try to open a window when run here, so
    # turn it off while the code runs and close the figures it made afterwards
    import sys
    pyplot = sys.modules.get("matplotlib.pyplot")
    if pyplot is not None:
        real_show = pyplot.show
        pyplot.show = lambda *args, **kwargs: None
    try:
        exec(compile(tree, "<exercise>", "exec"), __main__.__dict__, user_vars)
    finally:
        if pyplot is not None:
            pyplot.show = real_show
            pyplot.close("all")
    if expr is not None:
        user_vars["__check_result__"] = eval(expr, __main__.__dict__, user_vars)
        var = "__check_result__"
    for name in list(defines) + [var]:
        if name not in user_vars:
            raise NameError(name + " not defined")
    return user_vars[var]

def values_match(actual, expected):
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd
    if isinstance(expected, (tuple, list)):
        if not isinstance(actual, (tuple, list, np.ndarray)) or len(actual) != len(expected):
            return False
        # (compared here directly: values_match cannot call itself, since py_run_string keeps its name local)
        try:
            return all(bool(np.isclose(float(a), float(e))) for a, e in zip(actual, expected))
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            return False
    if isinstance(expected, (pd.Series, pd.DataFrame)):
        actual, expected = [
            x.squeeze(axis=1) if isinstance(x, pd.DataFrame) and x.shape[1] == 1 else x
            for x in (actual, expected)
        ]
        if type(actual) is not type(expected):
            return False
        actual, expected = actual.sort_index(), expected.sort_index()
        if list(actual.index) != list(expected.index):
            return False
        if isinstance(expected, pd.DataFrame):
            last_level = lambda cols: [c[-1] if isinstance(c, tuple) else c for c in cols]
            if last_level(actual.columns) != last_level(expected.columns):
                return False
        try:
            return bool(np.allclose(actual.to_numpy(dtype=float), expected.to_numpy(dtype=float), equal_nan=True))
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            return False
    try:
        return bool(np.isclose(float(actual), float(expected)))
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return False
'

custom_checker <- function(label, user_code, solution_code, check_code, envir_result, evaluate_result, envir_prep, last_value, stage, ...) {
  # (learnr doesn't pass the last value of Python chunks, so we run the code)
  if (label %in% names(value_checks)) {
    if (stage != "check") return()
    spec <- value_checks[[label]]
    correct <- tryCatch({
      helpers <- reticulate::py_run_string(checker_py, local = TRUE, convert = FALSE)
      get_result <- function(code) {
        helpers$get_result(code, var = spec$var, expr = spec$expr,
                           last_value = isTRUE(spec$last_value), defines = as.list(spec$defines))
      }
      values_match <- helpers$values_match
      # Student's code runs first, so if it modifies shared data the solution can't fill it in for them
      actual <- get_result(user_code)
      expected <- if (is.null(spec$value)) get_result(solution_code) else reticulate::r_to_py(spec$value)
      isTRUE(reticulate::py_to_r(values_match(actual, expected)))
    }, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (correct) {
      return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
    }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
  # Exact code checking (requires a <label>-solution chunk and <label>-code-check chunk)
  if (stage == "code_check") {
      if (user_code == solution_code){
          return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
      }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
}

gradethis_setup()
tutorial_options(exercise.completion = FALSE, exercise.checker = custom_checker,
                 exercise.reveal_solution = FALSE)
```

```{js mcq-cooldown, echo=FALSE}
// Cooldown on the "Try Again" button of multiple choice questions (radio buttons or
// checkboxes; numeric questions are not affected). The wait is 10 seconds after the first
// wrong answer to a question and 10 seconds longer after each one after that, up to 60.
// Attempts are saved in the browser so reloading the page doesn't reset the countdown.
(function() {
  var FIRST_WAIT = 10, EXTRA_WAIT = 10, MAX_WAIT = 60;  // seconds
  // The page title is part of the key so labs served from the same address (like
  // localhost) don't share each other's attempts
  var KEY = "mcq-cooldown:" + window.location.pathname + ":" + document.title;
  var state = {};
  try { state = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY)) || {}; } catch (e) {}
  function save() { try { localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(state)); } catch (e) {} }
  var justSubmitted = {};

  // When a multiple choice answer is submitted, note it, so that a Try Again button
  // showing up afterwards counts as a new wrong attempt (and one that shows up after a
  // page reload doesn't)
  document.addEventListener("click", function(e) {
    var btn = e.target.closest && e.target.closest('button.btn-primary[id$="-action_button"]');
    var question = btn && btn.closest(".tutorial-question");
    if (question && question.querySelector('input[type="radio"], input[type="checkbox"]')) {
      justSubmitted[question.getAttribute("data-label")] = true;
    }
  }, true);

  function startCooldown(btn) {
    var question = btn.closest(".tutorial-question");
    if (!question || btn.dataset.cooldown) return;
    var id = question.getAttribute("data-label");
    if (justSubmitted[id]) {
      delete justSubmitted[id];
      var attempts = (state[id] ? state[id].attempts : 0) + 1;
      var wait = Math.min(FIRST_WAIT + EXTRA_WAIT * (attempts - 1), MAX_WAIT);
      state[id] = { attempts: attempts, until: Date.now() + wait * 1000 };
      save();
    }
    if (!state[id]) return;  // not a multiple choice question
    btn.dataset.cooldown = "true";
    var label = btn.textContent;
    (function tick() {
      var secondsLeft = Math.ceil((state[id].until - Date.now()) / 1000);
      if (secondsLeft > 0 && document.body.contains(btn)) {
        btn.disabled = true;
        btn.textContent = label + " (" + secondsLeft + "s)";
        setTimeout(tick, 250);
      } else {
        btn.disabled = false;
        btn.textContent = label;
      }
    })();
  }

  // learnr adds a new Try Again button (yellow, btn-warning) each time an answer is wrong
  var selector = 'button.btn-warning[id$="-action_button"]';
  new MutationObserver(function(mutations) {
    mutations.forEach(function(m) {
      m.addedNodes.forEach(function(node) {
        if (!node.querySelectorAll) return;
        if (node.matches(selector)) startCooldown(node);
        node.querySelectorAll(selector).forEach(startCooldown);
      });
    });
  }).observe(document.documentElement, { childList: true, subtree: true });
})();
```

## Goals

The goal of this lab is to review confidence intervals, complete with an example of a $t$-interval. 

## Setup

This lab will use `numpy`, `pandas`, `scipy.stats`, and `statistics`. You may also want to use your favorite graphics packages (`matplotlib`, `seaborn`, or `plotnine`). Run this cell to load the packages. 

```{python packages, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}
import numpy as np 
import pandas as pd
import scipy.stats as st 
import statistics 

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn
import plotnine as p9
```

## A Review of Parameters and Statistics

Hypothesis tests are a form of statistical inference, but before we review the specifics, let's take a step back. 

Remember that a **population** is a complete group of all cases, subjects, or observations of interest. 
Summaries of various numerical characteristics of a population are known as **parameters**. 

For various reasons, we can't always gather information on an entire population (known as a census). Instead, we usually work with a **sample** of data, where a sample is defined as a subset of the cases, subjects, or observations in a given population.
Once you have acquired a sample, you can calculate a **statistic**. A statistic describes a numerical characteristic of a sample, and the intent is to use them to estimate the population parameter. 

If you need a refresher on any of these terms, refer back to the Data Collection and Visualization lab, where we discussed populations, samples, parameters, and statistics in more detail.

## Point Estimates

Let's look at some statistics in practice. The data frame `state_x77_df` contains data on all 50 United States from the 1970s, with one row per state and eight variables:

* `Population`: population estimate as of July 1, 1975 (in thousands)
* `Income`: per capita income in 1974 (in dollars)
* `Illiteracy`: percent of the population that was illiterate in 1970
* `Life Exp`: life expectancy in years (1969--71)
* `Murder`: murder and non-negligent manslaughter rate per 100,000 people (1976)
* `HS Grad`: percent of the population that were high-school graduates in 1970
* `Frost`: mean number of days with a minimum temperature below freezing (1931--1960) in the capital or a large city
* `Area`: land area in square miles

Rather than calculating each statistic one at a time, `pandas` gives us a shortcut: the `.describe()` method, which calculates several summary statistics for every numeric column of a data frame at once. ### Point Estimate Definition

What do all of these values have in common? Statistics like $\bar{x}$, etc., are called **point estimates**--they are all single values or points. 

Imagine that you are looking for a single red marble in an infinite sea of blue marbles. If you take one single marble, it is almost impossible to choose the red one. **Similarly, we are very unlikely to capture the exact value for the parameter (theoretically, the probability is zero)**. 

If you take a large group of marbles, you are more likely to find the red one, even if you have many extra blue marbles. Many statisticians then prefer to use an **interval estimate**, which provides a range of values and is therefore more likely to capture the parameter of interest.  

## Confidence Intervals

Statistical inference is the idea of **making inferences or drawing conclusions** about the parameters based on our samples of data, which we summarize with statistics (i.e., the sample mean, a sample proportion, etc.). There are two "flavors" of statistical inference, that you might be familiar with:

* **Confidence Intervals** provide a range of reasonable values for a parameter given a dataset.
* **Hypothesis Tests** check to see if a dataset is consistent with a previously held belief or a given value for the population paramete (more on this next week!)

These two flavors are related, but this lab focuses on confidence intervals. In contrast to a point estimate, an **interval estimate** gives us information about the variability of a statistic--that is, how much change we can expect in the statistic if we take a new sample. When we construct a confidence interval (a type of interval estimate), we are making statements about parameters (like the population mean $\mu$) that incorporate information about the **sampling variability**. **Confidence intervals are always statements about parameters**--there is no need to build an interval for a statistic, as we know exactly what values those take on. So, more technically, a confidence interval can be thought of as a range of reasonable values for a parameter based on the sample statistics.

### Sampling Distributions

To build our confidence interval, we will need something called the **sampling distribution**. The sampling distribution tells you what values the statistic will take and how often they occur. Why do we need a sampling distribution? Remember--we are calculating the statistic from a (hopefully random) sample. However, different samples will result in different statistics, so we are expecting some variability. The sampling distribution gives us a mathematical way to describe that variability.

We rely heavily on the Central Limit Theorem to find a sampling distribution. For a mean, the Central Limit Theorem states that when observations are independent and the sample size $n$ is sufficiently large, the sample average $\bar{x}$ will tend to follow a normal distribution with mean

$$\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu_X$$

and standard error

$$SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma_X}{\sqrt{n}}$$

In other words, the sample mean has the following distribution:

$$N\bigg(\mu_X, \frac{\sigma_X}{\sqrt{n}}\bigg)$$

However, if we do not know the mean $\mu_X$ for a variable, we are not very likely to know the variables standard deviation, $\sigma_X$. Often, we have to estimate $\sigma_X$ with the sample standard deviation, $s$. Because of the extra uncertainty, we usually use what is called a $t$-distribution instead of the normal distribution. The $t$-distribution has slightly thicker tails than a normal distribution, which helps us account for the extra uncertainty we introduced by using $s$ to estimate $\sigma_X$--you can see a few different $t$-distributions in the image below:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.width=8, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(latex2exp)

ggplot(data = data.frame(x = c(-3, 3)), aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), aes(color = "line1")) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, n = 101, args = list(df = 1), aes(color = "line2")) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, n = 101, args = list(df = 2), aes(color = "line3")) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, n = 101, args = list(df = 4), aes(color = "line4")) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, n = 101, args = list(df = 8), aes(color = "line5")) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, n = 101, args = list(df = 16), aes(color = "line6")) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, n = 101, args = list(df = 24), aes(color = "line7")) +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#A4343A", "#DE7C00", "#EAAA00", "#789D4A", "#275D38", "#007396", "#59315F"), labels = unname(TeX(c("Normal", "$t_1$", "$t_2$", "$t_4$", "$t_8$", "$t_{16}$", "$t_{24}$", "$t_{32}$")))) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())
```

$t$-Distributions are fairly close to the standard normal distribution, as you saw in the graph above. Similarly to the standard normal, the $t$-distribution is centered around zero and is also symmetric, so $P(T < -t) = P(T > t)$. Unlike the standard normal, the $t$-distribution is defined by only one parameter known as the degrees of freedom (`df` in the methods above). The smaller the degrees of freedom, the thicker the tails of the distribution. The larger the degrees of freedom, the closer to the normal distribution.

Typically in a confidence interval, we are trying to find the middle 95% of the values. This is equivalent to finding the $2.5^{th}$ and $97.5^{th}$ percentiles of the sampling distribution. 

```{r echo = F, fig.height = 4}

 scale_y_continuous(name = unname(TeX("$p(t)$")), limits = c(0, 0.42)) + 
 theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.y=element_blank(), text = element_text(size=20), axis.text.x = element_text(hjust=1))

```

### Confidence Interval Framework

Once you've determined a confidence interval is the correct procedure, there are four steps to building it:

1. **Prepare**. Identify the parameter of interest, identify the confidence level, and identify relevant sample statistics.

2. **Check**. Verify conditions to ensure a confidence interval can be used. These conditions will depend on the exact procedure, but at minimum, we are assuming that the observations are independent.

3. **Calculate**. If the conditions hold, compute the standard error, the margin of error, and the resulting interval.

4. **Conclude**. State the final confidence interval, and *provide an interpretation in the context of the problem*.

This last step is super important!! We want to make sure that we can communicate the results to a general audience, and not just people that have statistical training. Make sure you include this whenever you write up a confidence interval.

## Confidence Interval Example

In April 2020, McDonald's [transitioned to a limited menu to simplify tasks for restaurant workers and safely serve customers during the coronavirus public health crisis](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2020/06/19/mcdonalds-coronavirus-menu/). By transitioning to a limited menu and simplifying tasks, the company hoped that interaction times between customers and staff would be shorter, giving the virus less time to move between hosts.

A McDonald's franchise owner wished to take a data-driven approach to business, and came to you with a sample of data from the drive-through trips at their location.

### Prepare

The franchise owner would like to know what a reasonable value for the true mean drive through wait time (in seconds) might be, based on the sample of their data.

```{r q24, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "What should our confidence interval be about?",
  answer("$\\mu$, the mean drive-through wait time for all orders at the franchise owner's location.", correct = TRUE),
  answer("$\\bar{x}$, the mean drive-through wait time from our sample of trips", message = "Don't forget! The interval should be about a parameter, not a statistic."),
  answer("$p$, the proportion of drive-through wait times that decreased", message = "Don't forget! Our interval is about a mean, not a proportion."),
answer("$\\hat{p}$, the proportion of drive-through wait times that decreased in our sample"),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,

)
```

### Check

The next step is to check. For a "traditional" piece of inference like a $t$-interval for the mean, we tend to check two things:

1. First, we check to see if the distribution of the sample mean is normal. The best way to do this is to check the distribution of the original data, using a histogram--if the original distribution is normal, the Central Limit Theorem will kick in faster, and we can safely assume the sampling distribution is normal as well.

Create a histogram using the sample.

```{python histogram, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

```

```{r q27, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "Check all options that apply to the shape of this histogram.",
  answer("Uniform"),
  answer("Unimodal", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Bimodal"),
  answer("Multimodal"),
  answer("Symmetric", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Right-Skewed"),
  answer("Left-Skewed"),
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

Normal distributions are symmetric and unimodal (also often called "bell-shaped")--this data is normal, and therefore, we are safe in assuming that the sampling distribution is also normal.

2. Next, we assume the data are independent from each other, that is, no one observation gives us any information about the others. There is no good way to check independence other than to look at the context of the data. In this case, the franchise owner has assured us the sample is random, and therefore, we are again safe in assuming the data is independent.

### Calculate

Now, we use our formulas to calculate the standard error, margin of error, and the interval. Remember, the formula for the standard error in a $t$-test for the mean is

$$\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

Implement this formula in the cell below, and save the standard error as `se_mcds`.

```{python se, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}

```

```{python se-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
se_mcds = std_mcds/np.sqrt(len(mcds))
```

```{r se-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```

Now we need to calculate the margin of error. Remember that the formula for the margin of error is

$$t^*_{df} \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

where $t^*_{n-1}$ depends on two quantities:

* The confidence level, and
* The degrees of freedom, $df$.

First, let's focus on the confidence level. Earlier, we said that we would like to use a confidence level of 95\%, which means we are looking for an interval that contains 95\% of the sampling distribution. From the previous section, that means we are looking for the $97.5^{th}$ percentile. 

<!-- ```{r q7, echo=FALSE} -->
<!-- question( -->
<!--   "If 95% of the sampling distribution is contained within the interval, how much of the interval is outside of the interval?", -->
<!--   answer("95%", message = "There should be 95% inside the interval, not outside."),  -->
<!--   answer("5%", correct = TRUE),  -->
<!--   answer("2.5%", message = "There should be 2.5% on either side of the interval, but 5% overall."),  -->
<!--   answer("No way to tell."),  -->
<!--   random_answer_order = TRUE, -->
<!--   allow_retry = TRUE,  -->
<!--   post_message = "Congratulations! You have found the fourth secret word: " -->
<!-- ) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Remember that the area outside the interval should fall equally on both sides of the area inside, which is centered at the sample mean.  -->


```{r q28, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "True or False: We could also use the $2.5^{th}$ percentile.",
  answer("True", correct = TRUE),
  answer("False"),
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

::: {.center}

How do you know the answers to the previous question? Make sure you can justify your response!

::::

Now, let's focus on on the degrees of freedom. Traditionally in a $t$-interval for a single mean, the degrees of freedom is the sample size minus 1--this is why it is important to state the sample size in the Prepare step! 

```{r q29, echo=FALSE}
question_numeric(
  "What is the correct degrees of freedom to use?",
  answer(63, correct = TRUE),
  min = 1,
  max = 100,
  step = 1,
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

Now, find the value of $t$ we should be using in the interval--call it $t^*$, or `t_star`. 

```{python ex30, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}

```

```{python ex30-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
t_star = t.ppf(0.975, df = 63)
```

```{r ex30-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```

Now, combine the `t_star` and `se_mcds` to find the margin of error. Save it as `MoE_mcds`.

```{python ex31, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}

```

```{python ex31-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
MoE_mcds = se_mcds*t_star
```

```{r ex31-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```

Now, we can calculate the final interval by adding and subtracting the margin of error from the sample mean. Carry out these calculations below, and save the lower and upper bounds of the interval as `lower_mcds` and `upper_mcds`:

```{python ex32, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}

```

```{python ex32-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
lower_mcds = mean_mcds - MoE_mcds
upper_mcds = mean_mcds + MoE_mcds
```

```{r ex32-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```

Once we have the interval, we also need to be interpreting it in the context of the problem.

```{r q33, echo=FALSE}
question(

  answer("We are 95% confident that the sample mean drive-through wait time for all orders at the franchise owner's location.", message = "Of course the sample mean is between 216 and 257--we used the sample mean to build the interval! We can be 100% confident!"),
  answer("There is a 95% chance that the true mean drive-through wait time for all orders at the franchise owner's location is between 216 and 257 seconds.", message = "This is not what the word confident means in this case--be careful to use its proper definition."),
  answer("If we built 100 confidence intervals using this exact procedure with different samples from the franchise owner's location, approximately 95 of them would contain true mean drive-through wait time for all McDonald's at the franchise owner's location.", correct = TRUE),
  answer("95% of the observations are between 216 and 257 seconds."),
```

### Using `scipy.stats` Functions

There is a somewhat faster way to build the $t$-interval, and, if you are not comfortable with the math, it can also be more user-friendly. Look up the [documentation for `t.interval()`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.t.html). Unfortunately, you do still have to calculate the mean and standard error, but since we have those, you can plug them straight into the method--make sure you look up any other arguments you may need.

```{python ex34, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}

```

```{python ex34-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
t.interval(0.95, 63, loc=mean_mcds, scale=se_mcds)
```

```{r ex34-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```
